title: Supernova Nears Peak: Brightness Could Settle Galaxy NGC 1433 Distance, 30 or 62 Million Light-Years
excerpt: Supernova NGC 1433 observers are watching for the peak of SN 2026ahvu, a Type Ia explosion whose brightness could decide whether the galaxy sits about 30 or 62 million light-years away. content:
SN 2026ahvu, a white dwarf that exploded in the spiral galaxy NGC 1433 about 50 million light-years away (roughly 294 quintillion miles), is inside its forecast peak window, which opened Nov. 18 and runs through Monday, Nov. 23. The brightness it reaches could decide which published distance to the galaxy is right, because estimates range from about 30 to 62 million light-years.

Coverage dated as late as Nov. 19 describes the supernova as still approaching its expected maximum, though that wording echoes NOIRLab's release rather than new measurements. The latest dated brightness reading is an amateur estimate of magnitude 12.3 on Nov. 12, slightly fainter than the 12.1 faint end of the forecast range.

A separate preprint posted Nov. 6 adds a second reason to watch: it places the explosion beside star clusters younger than 100 million years, which would make SN 2026ahvu a "prompt" Type Ia supernova if the link holds. The preprint has not been peer reviewed. From US territory, only far southern latitudes can see the object, and a bright Moon complicates it, so most US readers will follow it through observatory data rather than a backyard telescope.

Published Distances to NGC 1433 Span 30 to 62 Million Light-Years

The preprint quotes two published distances and declines to pick one. The first is 9.1 megaparsecs (about 30 million light-years), measured from the tip of the red giant branch by Sabbi and colleagues in 2018, a figure flagged as quite uncertain. The second is 18.9 megaparsecs (about 62 million light-years), from the planetary nebula luminosity function, a method that uses the brightness of glowing planetary nebulae, published by Scheuermann and colleagues in 2022.

A third figure sits between them: 14.2 megaparsecs (about 46 million light-years), from a 2020 red giant branch analysis of Hubble data by Tikhonov and Galazutdinova. Startgaze reports that the 2020 study argues the earlier result mistook a different class of stars for the red giant tip. NOIRLab adopts about 50 million light-years and says published estimates differ.

Peak Magnitude Maps to Distance: Near 10.5 Means Close, Near 12.1 Means Far

Type Ia supernovae work as distance markers because carbon-oxygen white dwarfs explode near a common critical mass of about 1.44 solar masses, which gives the blasts nearly the same intrinsic peak brightness. Astronomers compare that known output with how bright the explosion appears, and the inverse-square law converts the gap into distance. A correction based on how fast the light curve fades, called the Phillips relation, tightens the match. The cosmic distance ladder entry puts current uncertainty near 5 percent, or 0.1 magnitudes. NOIRLab says observing the maximum apparent brightness will improve what is known about the distance to NGC 1433.

Startgaze, an observing-guide site, applied that logic to NGC 1433. Assuming a peak absolute V-band magnitude of −19.3, it predicts a peak near magnitude 10.5 at the 29-million-light-year distance and near 11.5 to 11.6 at the 46 to 49 million light-year distances. The same distance-modulus arithmetic gives about 12.1 at the 62-million-light-year figure (calculated), which matches the faint end of NOIRLab's forecast range of magnitude 10.5 to 12.1. NOIRLab's release does not say how it derived that range, so the match is an observation, not NOIRLab's stated method.

Two limits apply. The mapping shifts with the assumed absolute magnitude: SN 2011fe in the Pinwheel Galaxy peaked near magnitude 9.9 at about 21 million light-years, which corresponds to an absolute magnitude near −19, so adopting that value would make every predicted peak about 0.3 magnitudes fainter (calculated). NOIRLab also says peak timing varies by filter. Even so, Startgaze puts Type Ia scatter near 0.15 magnitudes after light-curve correction, small next to the roughly 1.6 magnitudes separating the nearest and farthest published distances (calculated), so a clean peak measurement could discriminate between them.

Latest Dated Reading Is Magnitude 12.3 on Nov. 12, and No Peak Is Confirmed

ATLAS, the Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System, logged the object on Nov. 2 at about 04:20 UTC (11:20 p.m. ET on Nov. 1) at magnitude 17.06. The GOTO survey recorded a marginal detection on Nov. 1 at 12:58 UTC (7:58 a.m. ET) and nothing on Oct. 30, which puts first light inside a window of about two days. NOIRLab reports the object reached about magnitude 13.5 within days. On the magnitude scale, where lower numbers are brighter, the climb from 17 to 13.5 is a jump of about 25 times in brightness (calculated; each magnitude step is a factor of about 2.512).

Amateur V-band measurements compiled on David Bishop's Bright Supernovae page, from observer Pepe Manteca, show magnitude 15.9 on Nov. 3, 13.9 on Nov. 6, 12.6 on Nov. 10 and 12.3 on Nov. 12. That is about three times brighter than the 13.5 figure NOIRLab cited (calculated). Startgaze applies a mean rise time near 19 days, from Firth and colleagues in 2015, to a first-light date near Nov. 1 and estimates a peak around Nov. 19 to 20. That is an estimate. As of Nov. 20, the sources cited here report no confirmed peak.

Preprint Places Explosion Beside Star Clusters Younger Than 100 Million Years

The preprint, posted to arXiv on Nov. 6, submitted to The Astrophysical Journal Letters and led by Sumit K. Sarbadhicary, used Hubble and James Webb Space Telescope images to examine the explosion site. Two ultraviolet-bright clusters sit 0.19 and 0.26 arcseconds from the supernova, which works out to roughly 26 to 78 light-years depending on which galaxy distance is correct (calculated from the preprint's 8 to 24 parsecs). The authors fit the northern cluster at 37 million years old using Hubble and Webb data (57 million with Hubble alone) and the southern cluster at 95 million years (88 million).

The age matters because of Type Ia delay time, the gap between a white dwarf's birth and its explosion. The preprint describes a prompt component with delays of a few hundred million years and a delayed component of billions of years, and says population models typically predict a minimum delay near 100 million years for white-dwarf mergers and for companion-fed systems with non-degenerate partners, and about 40 million years when the companion is hydrogen-stripped. The authors write that association with either cluster would make SN 2026ahvu a prompt case, because even the older cluster's 95 million years falls under 100 million.

The authors put the chance of an unrelated Type Ia landing this close to a cataloged cluster at about 0.4 percent, rising to about 4 percent if any significant near-ultraviolet emission counts. Closeness on the sky does not prove a physical link. The preprint carries both galaxy distances without choosing one, and the cluster separations change with the distance adopted while the ages do not, so the peak measurement bears on the physical separations. Which route a given white dwarf took, gaining matter from a companion or merging with another white dwarf, also remains unsettled.

DECam, Gemini South and SOAR Are Tracking Color, Brightness and Composition

NOIRLab says the Dark Energy Camera (DECam) on the 4-meter (13-foot) Víctor M. Blanco Telescope at Cerro Tololo in Chile, Gemini South and the SOAR telescope on Cerro Pachón are observing the supernova, and it has invited other observatories to add complementary observations. Planned work includes repeated imaging to track brightness and color, plus spectroscopy to measure what the expanding material is made of. NOIRLab calls the early catch a valuable chance to study the explosion as it unfolds, and says SN 2026ahvu is one of the nearest Type Ia since SN 2011fe appeared in 2011, which sat at about 21 million light-years.

DECam also imaged NGC 1433 before the explosion during the Dark Energy Survey, a survey led by DOE's Fermilab that ran from 2013 to 2019, so astronomers can compare the site before and after. The Department of Energy funded the camera, which was built and tested at Fermilab. Gemini South's data come from Director's Discretionary Program GS-2026B-DD-104. S. Dahm of NSF NOIRLab/Gemini is principal investigator for the Gemini image, and G. Narayan and T. Murphey of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign are principal investigators for the DECam images.

Universe Today says spectra taken two to three months after the explosion, once the debris thins, should reveal the composition of the whole exploded star. That points to roughly January or early February 2027 (calculated from a first-light date near Nov. 1).

Can You See SN 2026ahvu From US Latitudes?

Only from the far south, and only with equipment. NOIRLab says the supernova is visible in small to moderately sized amateur telescopes under favorable conditions, particularly from southern locations, as a faint point of light, and that imaging can reveal it with smaller telescopes than visual observing needs. People far north may find it difficult or impossible. IFLScience says the host galaxy rises only a few degrees above the horizon for many Northern Hemisphere observers.

Startgaze gives the maximum altitude as 90 degrees minus the observer's latitude minus 47.1 degrees, at the galaxy's highest point in the sky, and says the galaxy never rises north of about 43 degrees north. Applying that formula (calculated) gives roughly 22 degrees above the horizon from Honolulu, 24 from San Juan, 17 from Miami, 13 from Houston, 9 from Los Angeles and 2 from New York, which is too low for any practical viewing.

At forecast brightness the object is far fainter than the roughly magnitude 6.5 naked-eye limit. Visual limits at high magnification run near magnitude 12.3 for a 60-millimeter (2.4-inch) telescope and 13.3 for a 102-millimeter (4-inch) telescope in good conditions. The host galaxy's glow, about magnitude 10 spread across roughly 6.5 by 5.9 arcminutes, can make the point harder to pick out than its magnitude suggests, and Startgaze says a gibbous Moon 63 to 99 percent lit is up near culmination each night from Nov. 18 through the forecast peak window.

Measured Peak Near 10.5, 11.5 or 12.1 Would Favor Different Distances

Under the absolute-magnitude assumption above (calculated), a reported peak near magnitude 10.5 would favor about 30 million light-years, a peak near 11.5 to 11.6 would favor the 46 to 49 million light-year estimates, and a peak near 12.1 would favor 62 million. Because peak timing varies by filter, the number that matters will depend on which filter a measurement uses.

Readers who want to judge the result themselves now have the conversion: a brighter peak means a closer galaxy, a fainter one means a farther galaxy, and the preprint's prompt-explosion claim stays a candidate until peer review and further data test it.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a Type Ia supernova?

It is the destruction of a white dwarf, the dense remnant of a Sun-like star that packs roughly the Sun's mass into an Earth-size volume, after the white dwarf gains matter from a companion or merges with another white dwarf.

Has the "prompt" Type Ia claim been confirmed?

No. It comes from an arXiv preprint submitted to a journal and not yet peer reviewed, and its title says only that the supernova "may be" prompt.

Where can the public find the professional observations?

NOIRLab published its release and images, and Gemini South's observations fall under program GS-2026B-DD-104, the identifier to look up in the Gemini Observatory Archive; whether that data is public yet is unconfirmed. Amateur light-curve readings are compiled on David Bishop's Bright Supernovae page.

Has NGC 1433 hosted a supernova before?

Yes. SN 1985P, a Type II supernova that reached magnitude 13.5, was discovered there by Robert Evans on Oct. 10, 1985.
